summary: This document extends BGP-LS to advertise BGP Peering Segments with their peering node information, so efficient Egress Peer Engineering policies can be computed using Segment Routing. A segment is an instruction, and a list of segment identifiers steers a packet.

eli5.summary: A network can choose which exit door to use to a neighbor. This document lets the doors be announced as segments so a planner can choose where traffic leaves.

questions: what is bgp egress peer engineering
subtitle: How BGP-LS announces the Segment Routing labels a router uses to steer traffic out to a chosen BGP peer.

tldr.problem: To choose which egress router and which external BGP peer a flow leaves through, a controller needs to learn the peering topology and the Segment Routing identifiers for each peer.
tldr.mechanism: BGP-LS Link NLRI with a new Protocol-ID for BGP carries the BGP peering topology, and three new Link Attribute TLVs carry the PeerNode, PeerAdj and PeerSet SIDs.
tldr.outcome: Controllers can compute Egress Peer Engineering policies from this information. It is a Proposed Standard, not obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9086 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The controller-based use of these segments is illustrated in RFC 9087.

sections.title: Segment Routing and Egress Peer Engineering
sections.content:
In Segment Routing (SR), a node steers a packet through a controlled set of instructions called segments by prepending a list of segment identifiers (SIDs). A SID can represent any instruction, topological or service based, and per-flow state is kept only at the ingress node of the SR domain.

This document extends BGP-LS, defined in RFC 7752, to advertise BGP Peering Segments together with the peering topology: a node's peers, interfaces and peering Autonomous Systems. The goal is to let a controller compute efficient BGP Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE) policies using the SR-MPLS data plane. The corresponding SRv6 extensions are specified in a separate Internet-Draft.

RFC 9087 illustrates the centralized controller use case, where the controller learns the Peering SIDs through BGP-LS and programs a policy at any node in the domain to steer traffic via a specific egress node to specific External BGP (EBGP) peers.
sections.eli5: A planner wants to decide which exit door each trip uses. First the planner has to be told where the doors are and what they are called.

sections.title: The Three BGP Peering Segments
sections.content:
The SR architecture (RFC 8402) defines three BGP Peering Segments that an egress Provider Edge node can instantiate for its attached peers:

  • PeerNode SID: steer to a specific peer node.
  • PeerAdj SID: steer over a specific local interface towards a specific peer node.
  • PeerSet SID: load-balance across a set of peer nodes.

Each BGP session MUST be described by a PeerNode SID. The description MAY be augmented by additional PeerAdj SIDs for the underlying links, and PeerNode or PeerAdj SIDs MAY be grouped under a common PeerSet SID. At minimum, a policy applied at an ingress PE uses two SIDs: the Node SID of the chosen egress PE, then the Peering SID for the chosen peer or peering interface.

The extensions could be used for Internal BGP (IBGP) sessions too, but a BGP router SHOULD NOT instantiate a Peering SID for sessions to peers that are not in the forwarding path, such as route reflectors, since the purpose of the SID is to steer traffic to that peer.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of door names: one for a neighbor, one for one particular road to that neighbor, and one for a whole group of neighbors where traffic is shared out.

sections.title: Describing BGP Peering in BGP-LS NLRI
sections.content:
Peering information is advertised in the BGP-LS Link NLRI type, using a new Protocol-ID 7 meaning BGP. The new ID keeps these NLRIs separate from those carrying IGP link-state information defined in RFC 7752.

Two new Node Descriptor TLVs are defined: BGP Router-ID (type 516, 4 octets, the BGP Identifier from RFC 6286) and Member-ASN (type 517, 4 octets, the Member-AS Number from RFC 5065).

The local node descriptors MUST include the BGP Router-ID (516) and the Autonomous System Number (512, which holds the confederation identifier if confederations are used). The remote node descriptors MUST include the same two TLVs for the peer. Member-ASN (517) MAY be added if BGP confederations are used. Because RFC 6286 requires the BGP identifier to be unique within an AS and non-zero, the ASN and Router-ID pair is globally unique.
sections.eli5: Each router is listed by a unique ID card, and each entry says which two routers it connects.

sections.title: The Peering SID TLVs
sections.content:
Three new Link Attribute TLVs carry the SIDs: 1101 PeerNode SID, 1102 PeerAdj SID and 1103 PeerSet SID. They all share one format: Type, Length (7 or 8, depending on whether a SID index or a label is carried), a Flags octet, a Weight octet, a Reserved field and the SID/Label/Index.

The flags are V (the SID carries a label value; set by default), L (local significance; set by default), B (backup: the path is eligible for fast reroute protection) and P (persistent: the SID value stays the same across router restart and session or interface flap). The remaining bits are reserved, MUST be zero when originated and are ignored when received. Weight is used for load balancing.

The value is either a 3-octet local label, using the 20 rightmost bits, in which case V and L MUST be set, or a 4-octet index into the router's Segment Routing Global Block, in which case the SRGB MUST be advertised using RFC 9085. The SID values SHOULD be persistent across router restart.
sections.eli5: Each door name comes on a small card with a few yes/no boxes, a share number for how busy it should be, and the door's number itself.

sections.title: Advertising Each Kind of SID
sections.content:
A BGP router enabled for Egress Peer Engineering MUST include the PeerNode SID TLV in the BGP-LS Attribute for the Link NLRI of each of its peering sessions. PeerAdj SID and PeerSet SID TLVs MAY be included. All three have SR operation NEXT.

  • PeerNode SID: the next hop is the connected peering node. The link descriptors carry the IPv4 or IPv6 local and neighbor addresses used by the BGP session (TLVs 259 to 262).
  • PeerAdj SID: the next hop is the interface peer address. The link descriptors MUST include Link Local/Remote Identifiers (TLV 258), with 0 used by default when the remote identifier is unknown. Interface and neighbor address TLVs MAY be added.
  • PeerSet SID: the next hop is load-balancing across any connected interface to any peer in the set. The same SID value is included in the Link NLRI of every PeerNode or PeerAdj segment in the set.
sections.eli5: For each neighbor, the router lists the neighbor door. It may also list each road to that neighbor, and a group name that covers several neighbors.

sections.title: Manageability and Operation
sections.content:
Section 6 of RFC 7752 applies, so the syntactic checks for malformed Link-State NLRI and BGP-LS Attributes also cover these TLVs. Semantic checking is left to the consumer, such as a controller. An error in NLRI descriptor TLVs would be expected to make that NLRI update unusable, so it is discarded with an error log, while an error in Attribute TLVs would discard only that attribute.

The operator MUST be able to configure, enable and disable the advertisement of each of the three SIDs, and to control what is advertised to which peer. The peering information travels over a distinct BGP-LS session, kept isolated as RFC 7752 describes.

A BGP-EPE path bypasses the normal BGP best-path routing for that flow and any BGP routing policies on the egress router. The controller must ensure there is no looping or misrouting. Counters on the MPLS label of the Peering SID show traffic forwarded over an EPE path and can help find issues.
sections.eli5: Operators must be able to switch each kind of door name on or off. Using a special route skips the usual choice, so someone must watch that traffic does not go in circles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new procedures and TLVs, by themselves, do not change the BGP-LS security model of RFC 7752. BGP-EPE steers traffic leaving the administrative domain, so the peering information collected through BGP-LS must be limited to specific consumers in a secure manner.

Segment Routing operates within a trusted domain, and BGP-EPE policies are expected to be used entirely within that trusted SR domain, for example between multiple AS or domains within a single provider network. BGP-LS sessions must be isolated so the topology, including the new peering topology, is not advertised to an external BGP peering session outside the administrative domain.
sections.eli5: The map of your exit doors is private. Only the planners inside your own network should see it, never the neighbors.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 7 or 8, depending on SID index or label encoding.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: V, L, B and P flags plus reserved bits.

fields.name: Weight
fields.desc: Weight of the SID for load balancing.

fields.name: SID/Label/Index
fields.desc: Variable length: a 3-octet label or a 4-octet index.

items.label: Member-ASN
items.desc: Node Descriptor, 4 octets; registered as BGP Confederation Member.

items.label: PeerNode SID
items.desc: Steer to a specific peer node.

items.label: PeerAdj SID
items.desc: Steer over a specific link to a peer.

items.label: PeerSet SID
items.desc: Load-balance across a set of peers.
